newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Peters' popularity rating slides in NBR poll.
newsitem.headline: NZ Peters' popularity rating slides in NBR poll.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters' popularity continues to tumble since he became deputy prime minister, the National Business Review said on Friday.
The paper said its latest NBR-Consultus poll, taken between February 7 and 11, showed Peters was now by far the most unpopular political leader. Two out of three adults gave him the thumbs down.

Peters' standing in the poll slumped a further six points since the coalition deal between his New Zealand First party and the conservative National party was signed in December. Now just 27 percent have a somewhat favourable or very favourable view of
him, compared with a 66 percent total unfavourability rating.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger lifted his favourability rating two points to 48 percent. He trails Labour leader Helen Clark at 56 percent, down three points since December.
Bolger rated unfavourably by 47 percent, while Clark was rated unfavourably by 39 percent.

Alliance leader Jim Anderton was rated favourably by 46 percent and unfavourably by 40 percent, while Act leader Richard Prebble was rated unfavourably by 55 percent (down three on December) and favourably by less than 30 percent.
Political news in the weeks leading up to the poll was dominated by debate about the Kiwi dollar and allegations about Maori television station Aotearoa Television News.
The poll does not take into account the public response to either Peters' first budget policy statement or his fracas with National MP John Banks this week.
NBR reported Peters' strongest critics were women, people aged under 30 and those earning NZ$15,000 or less a year.
Despite his unfavourable ratings, those polled believed Peters had more influence on the economy than Finance Minister Bill Birch.
Half of those polled said New Zealand First fared better out of the coalition agreement, while 12 percent thought National did and 25 percent thought the deal was fair to both parties.
Despite that result, 46 percent believed National was more likely to call the shots in the government than NZ First.
The poll surveyed 750 people and had a margin of error of 3.5 percent. -- Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
